sections.passage: When a quantity is too large or too small compared with the base unit, it is first written in scientific notation and then with an SI prefix. The prefix is chosen so that the number lies between 0.1 and 1000; for example, the radius of the Sun, 6.96 × 10⁸ m, is written 696 Mm. There must be no space between the prefix and the unit symbol, only one prefix may be used at a time, and a power applies to the whole prefixed unit. While writing values, the number and the unit are separated by a space and unit symbols are never made plural.

sections.title: Very short answer questions. Answer in 30–50 words.

questions.q: Find the derived SI units of density and pressure.
questions.answer: Density = mass/volume, so its unit is kg/m³ = kg m⁻³. Pressure = force/area = (kg m s⁻²)/m² = kg m⁻¹ s⁻², which is called the pascal (Pa).

questions.q: Derive the SI unit of pressure in terms of base units.
questions.answer: Pressure = force/area. Force = mass × acceleration has the unit kg m s⁻², and area has the unit m². So the unit of pressure = kg m s⁻² / m² = kg m⁻¹ s⁻², called the pascal (Pa).

questions.q: Rewrite the following measurements without using SI prefixes: (i) 1 pm (ii) 12 Gm (iii) 1 nm (iv) 10 Tm.
questions.answer: (i) 1 pm = 10⁻¹² m (ii) 12 Gm = 12 × 10⁹ m = 1.2 × 10¹⁰ m (iii) 1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m (iv) 10 Tm = 10 × 10¹² m = 10¹³ m.

questions.q: State two differences between fundamental (base) and derived units with examples.
questions.answer: (1) Base units are only seven in number (e.g. metre, kilogram, second), while derived units are very many (e.g. m², m s⁻¹, newton). (2) Base units are independent of each other, while derived units are obtained by combining base units (e.g. newton = kg m s⁻²).

questions.q: Give the name and symbol of the SI prefix used for: (a) 10³ (b) 10⁻⁶ (c) 10⁹ (d) 10⁻².
questions.answer: (a) kilo, k (b) micro, μ (c) giga, G (d) centi, c.

questions.q: Find the derived SI units of (a) force and (b) work.
questions.answer: (a) Force = mass × acceleration → kg × m s⁻² = kg m s⁻², called newton (N). (b) Work = force × distance → kg m s⁻² × m = kg m² s⁻², called joule (J).

questions.q: State the SI units used while measuring: (i) electric current flowing through a heater (ii) temperature of a furnace (iii) length of a hockey playground (iv) amount of a substance.
Why can't parts of the human body be used for accurate measurement?
questions.answer: Body parts such as the hand span, foot or cubit differ in size from person to person, so the same object gives different results when different people measure it. Such units are arbitrary and the measurements cannot be reproduced, which leads to disputes, especially in trade.

questions.q: List the three essential characteristics of a good unit.
questions.answer: A unit should be (1) relevant to the quantity being measured (distance is not measured in kilograms), (2) convenient in size (kilometre for the distance between cities, not inch) and (3) well defined, so that it is understood by everyone in the same way.

sections.title: Short answer questions. Answer in 50–80 words.

questions.q: Write two differences between base units and derived units. Derive the SI unit of energy in terms of base units. What special name is given to this unit?
questions.answer: Base units are seven and independent of each other; derived units are many and are formed from base units. Energy (work) = force × displacement = (kg m s⁻²) × m = kg m² s⁻². This unit has the special name joule (J).

questions.q: (a) Define luminous intensity and write its SI unit and symbol. (b) Derive the SI unit of work in terms of base SI units.
questions.answer: (a) Luminous intensity is the amount of light emitted by a point source per second in a particular direction. Its SI unit is the candela, symbol cd. (b) Work = force × displacement = mass × acceleration × displacement → kg × m s⁻² × m = kg m² s⁻² (joule).

questions.q: (a) What are derived units? Name the physical quantity whose derived unit is s⁻¹ and write the special name of this unit. (b) Derive the SI unit of force in terms of base units.
questions.answer: (a) Units of quantities other than the seven base quantities, obtained by combining base units, are derived units. s⁻¹ is the unit of frequency; its special name is hertz (Hz). (b) Force = mass × acceleration = mass × (length/time²) → kg m s⁻², called newton (N).

questions.q: (a) Differentiate between base units and derived units. (b) Why do we need a standard unit to measure a physical quantity?
questions.answer: (a) Base units (seven, e.g. metre, kilogram, second) are independent; derived units (e.g. m s⁻¹, newton, joule) are obtained from base units. (b) A standard unit is the same for everyone, so measurements made by different people or in different places agree. This avoids confusion and disputes in trade and makes scientific work reproducible; body-part units vary from person to person.

questions.q: (a) Classify kelvin and newton as base or derived units and name the quantities they measure. (b) Derive the SI unit of pressure in terms of base units.
questions.answer: (a) Kelvin is a base unit (thermodynamic temperature); newton is a derived unit (force). (b) Pressure = force/area = kg m s⁻² / m² = kg m⁻¹ s⁻² (pascal).
questions.note: October 2022 gave two units to classify; kelvin and newton are used here as an example.

questions.q: Write any three rules for writing SI units, with an example of each.
questions.answer: (1) Leave a space between the number and the unit symbol: 100 mg, not 100mg. (2) Symbols are not made plural and do not take a full stop: 10 kg, not 10 kgs or 10 kg. (3) Symbols named after people begin with a capital letter, but the full name does not: 30.5 J or 30.5 joule, not 30.5 Joules. (Also: write 0.928 g, not .928 g; m s means metre second while ms means millisecond.)

sections.title: Long answer questions. Answer in 80–120 words.

questions.q: What is a unit? List the characteristics of a good unit. Why were units based on parts of the body given up, and how did standard units develop?
questions.answer: A unit is a standard quantity (scale) in terms of which a physical quantity is measured; value = number × unit. A good unit is relevant, convenient and well defined. Units such as the hand span, foot or cubit differ from person to person, so they were arbitrary and gave results that could not be reproduced, causing disputes in trade. Rulers fixed standards (Egyptian standard cubit, Henry I's yard), but these changed with rulers. After the French Revolution the decimal metric system was made, with standard metre and kilogram kept near Paris (Metre Convention, 1875). CGS and MKS systems followed, and in 1960 the International System of Units (SI) was adopted with seven base units, now defined by constants of nature (e.g. the metre through the speed of light).

questions.q: Name the seven base physical quantities with their SI units and symbols. What are SI prefixes and why are they needed? Write 6.96 × 10⁸ m and 5 × 10⁻¹¹ m using suitable prefixes.
questions.answer: Length – metre (m); mass – kilogram (kg); time – second (s); electric current – ampere (A); temperature – kelvin (K); amount of substance – mole (mol); luminous intensity – candela (cd). Many values are too large or too small compared with the base unit and are awkward even in scientific notation, so SI prefixes (kilo 10³, mega 10⁶, giga 10⁹, milli 10⁻³, micro 10⁻⁶, nano 10⁻⁹, pico 10⁻¹² …) are used, chosen so that the number lies between 0.1 and 1000. 6.96 × 10⁸ m = 696 Mm (or 0.696 Gm); 5 × 10⁻¹¹ m = 50 pm.
